subject: VPC observability: log routing, trace hooks, and export patterns
messages:
From: security@acme-corp.com
To: markus_klein@redwoodinference.com
Date: Sat, 20 Jun 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Observability for Redwood Private on our VPC — log/trace export options

Hi Markus,

Thanks for the demo last week. Our security team (cc'd) asked for a short architecture read on how Redwood Private would deliver observability (logs/metrics/traces) from instances running in our VPC into our existing tooling. Key constraints:
- No internet egress to third-party SaaS (we have an allowlist policy).
- All telemetry must be encrypted at-rest and in-flight; keys managed by our KMS.
- We need either direct SIEM ingestion (Splunk/ELK) or secure on-prem buffering (Kafka/S3).
- Sampling controls for traces and request correlation across our services are required.

Can you share recommended patterns, any required firewall/VPC endpoint rules, and minimal config examples? Also tell us about retention/reporting hooks and audit logs for compliance.

Thanks,
Jared Cole
Security Architect, Acme Corp
security@acme-corp.com
From: markus_klein@redwoodinference.com
To: security@acme-corp.com
Cc: hannah_schmitt@redwoodinference.com, laura_bennett@redwoodinference.com
Date: Sat, 20 Jun 2026 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Observability for Redwood Private on our VPC — log/trace export options

Jared —

Appreciate the clear constraints. Attached is a short patterns doc (observability-patterns-v1.pdf) and a starter routing policy (draft-routing-policy.yaml). High-level recommendations:

1) Agentless OTLP-forwarder (preferred in strict egress environments)
   - Run an OTEL collector as a sidecar/daemonset inside the customer's VPC.
   - Collector exports via internal VPC endpoints (Splunk HEC, Kafka, S3) — no public egress.
   - Benefits: consistent batching, buffering, and encryption; easier key management with your KMS.

2) Secure forwarder (when you prefer managed buffering)
   - Option to deploy Redwood's forwarder appliance in your subnet. For environments that forbid sidecars, the forwarder can be provisioned in a dedicated subnet and accept TLS connections from Redwood Private nodes.
   - Forwarder supports persistent local disk encryption and throttled egress to on-prem collectors.

3) Direct SIEM ingestion rules (Splunk/ELK/Sumo)
   - Use Splunk HEC over mTLS to an internal load balancer. Provide client certs via your KMS.
   - For ELK, send to internal Logstash/Kafka cluster; we recommend using a topic-per-namespace approach.

4) Tracing & correlation
   - Redwood exposes a request-id and span-id on all ingress/egress events. We recommend propagating X-Request-ID and traceparent headers.
   - Sampling is configurable at the collector and in the runtime: by default we sample 1% for high-traffic inference endpoints and 100% for admin/control-plane flows.

5) Audit and retention hooks
   - Audit events (auth, deploy, config-change) are written to an immutable audit log store (S3 or internal object store) with lifecycle policies you control.
   - We can emit SOC-2-ready audit bundles on-demand (export + verify signatures).

Network items (minimal):
- Allow outbound to internal SIEM endpoints on TLS ports (443/8088 for Splunk HEC) via VPC route table to the SIEM LB.
- If using S3 for batched exports, permit VPC endpoint and S3 PutObject to the approved bucket.
- Open port for OTLP receiver (4317) from Redwood nodes to your collector subnet.

Next steps: Hannah (cc) will follow up with a more detailed firewall matrix and sample OTEL config. Happy to set a short tech review with your ops team next week.

— Markus Klein
VP Product, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Observability for Redwood Private on our VPC — log/trace export options

Hi Jared / team — quick technical addendum. A few concrete config snippets and gotchas: 

- OTEL Collector config: use the batching + retry exporter with a small on-disk buffer (10-20GB) for spikes. Set exporter timeout to 60s and reliable backoff.
- Syslog vs OTLP: prefer OTLP for structured spans/metrics. Use syslog only for legacy parsers; that route loses structured tracing context unless you inject X-Request-ID into logs.
- TLS + mTLS: we recommend mTLS for Splunk HEC; for Kafka use SASL_SSL with client certs stored in your KMS.
- RBAC for access to audit logs: configure S3 bucket policies that only allow reads to a specific role and require MFA for deletions.

Attachment draft-routing-policy.yaml contains:
- IP ranges to allow between redwood subnets and your collector subnet
- Recommended listener ports (OTLP 4317; metrics 4318; Splunk HEC 8088; optional syslog 514/tcp)
- Example IAM role and bucket policy for audit exports

I'll add a sample OTEL pipeline and push to the shared drive if you want.

Hannah Schmitt
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: soojin_lee@redwoodinference.com

Jared — adding some notes on tracing hooks and correlation (short examples inline).

1) Correlation IDs: Redwood runtime sets an internal trace_id and span_id for every inference request. We expose these as headers:
   - X-Request-ID: global request uuid
   - traceparent: W3C trace context (trace-id/span-id/flags)

Example: when an app calls the Redwood endpoint we recommend:
   - client -> Redwood ingress: include traceparent header
   - Redwood runtime: attach span for model-invoke and emit span event for cache-hit/miss
   - OTEL collector: map span attributes to your vendor schema (service.name, model.name, prompt_id)

2) Sampling strategy (configurable):
   - Probabilistic sampling at collector (0.01–0.05 typical), with rule overrides for admin users and long-running sessions.
   - Tail-based sampling can be enabled if you want to keep low noise but preserve high-latency traces; collector needs 1–5s lookback buffer.

3) Low-latency hooks: to minimize overhead we emit sampling metadata in a lightweight log line (info) that includes request_id, latency_ms, and model_shard. This allows your SIEM to surface anomalies without full span export.

4) PII considerations: avoid putting full prompts in trace metadata. If you need to store prompt hashes, use a deterministic salted hash with your KMS salt and log only the hash.

On the config side I'll attach a minimal OTEL receiver snippet to the shared drive; happy to walk through mapping to Splunk fields.

— Soojin Lee
Principal Engineer, Runtime

Quick operational notes from the Dedicated/Private onboarding perspective: 

- Firewall & egress: For customers that disallow all public egress we recommend a dedicated observability subnet with a single NAT or egress appliance that is managed by the customer's infra team. Redwood's forwarder will talk only to internal endpoints; we do not require public IPs.
- Cert rotation: Plan for a cert rotation cadence (90 days) and provide a rotation endpoint/role we can call to retrieve client certs.
- Throttling: We'll implement per-tenant rate limits on telemetry to avoid storming your collectors during model rollouts.
- SLAs: For audit exports we can provide a certified export window (24h for export bundle delivery).

Please confirm if your ops team needs us to open a PR for your routing tables / security group rules — we can produce a one-click CloudFormation/Terraform snippet for the flow.

Best,
Laura Bennett
Director, Customer Operations
